prior_importants.description: SYMLINK_CHECK_SHELL walks the sed-normalized `$REL` (`LINK_REST=$REL`), but the Write tool opens the raw `file_path`. sed works line by line, so its `s#^\./##` strip also fires after an embedded newline, where it is not a path-equivalent rewrite. A sandboxed worker plants a symlink whose name ends in `<LF>.` and then Writes through it. The hook checks a different, nonexistent path, exits 0 on scope-in, and the unsandboxed Write follows the link to a compiled hook or to the main checkout's `.pupitre/project.yml`.

findings.description: Workers launch with `--setting-sources user`, so the operator's user `settings.json` in `claudeUserDir(repoPath)` is loaded next to the compiled `--settings` file. Claude Code joins array settings from every source instead of letting one replace the other. So a `sandbox.excludedCommands`, `sandbox.network.allowedDomains` or `sandbox.filesystem.allowWrite` in the operator's user settings is added to the worker's sandbox. The compiled `allowUnsandboxedCommands: false` and `strictAllowlist: true` do not stop this, because they are single values and only replace single values. The trigger is an operator whose user settings already hold, say, `"sandbox": {"excludedCommands": ["docker"]}`, which Claude Code's docs give as an example, and who then sets `workerSandbox: true`. A worker can then run `docker run -v "$HOME:/h" ...` or the excluded `git -c core.fsmonitor=...` outside the sandbox, with full home access and open network. With `allowedDomains: ["github.com"]`, the registry-only network limit fails silently. pup never reads the user `sandbox` block, and ADR 0191 lists neither a ceiling nor a follow-up for it. The only related follow-up is about a worktree-local settings file. The ADR states "no command may ask to leave the sandbox" and that `strictAllowlist` holds "because the settings arrive by `--settings`", but neither is true for such an operator.
findings.body:
**A `sandbox` block in the operator's user settings widens the compiled worker sandbox.**

`launchArgs` (`src/claude/session-runtime.service.ts:728-746`) starts workers with `--settings <compiled> --setting-sources user`, so the operator's own `settings.json` is loaded as well (decision 9). Claude Code concatenates array settings across sources and does not replace them. A user-level `sandbox.excludedCommands`, `sandbox.network.allowedDomains` or `sandbox.filesystem.allowWrite` is therefore added to the block compiled here. The scalars here cannot take those entries back out:

```ts
    enabled: true,
    failIfUnavailable: true,
    allowUnsandboxedCommands: false,
...
    network: {
      allowedDomains: WORKER_SANDBOX_DOMAINS,
      strictAllowlist: true,
```

- **`allowUnsandboxedCommands: false`** only turns off `dangerouslyDisableSandbox`. Commands in `excludedCommands` still run outside the sandbox. Take an operator with `"excludedCommands": ["docker"]` (the docs' example) or `["git"]` who then sets `workerSandbox: true`. Their worker can run `docker run -v "$HOME:/h" …` or `git -c core.fsmonitor='…' status` with no sandbox at all.
- **`strictAllowlist`** decides what happens to a host missing from the merged list. It does not decide which source's list counts. That is `allowManagedDomainsOnly`, which only managed settings can set. So a user `allowedDomains` entry quietly widens the network beyond the registries.
- **A user `allowWrite` entry** cannot reopen a compiled `denyWrite`, since a deny wins. It can still grant paths that no compiled entry names.

pup never reads the user `sandbox` key, and `excludedCommands` appears nowhere in `src/`. ADR 0191 has no ceiling or follow-up for this; the closest is the follow-up on a worktree-local settings file. The `workerSandbox` JSDoc (L1359-1367) and the ADR ("a worker cannot ask its way out", and the `--setting-sources user` reasoning for `strictAllowlist`) are therefore wrong for such an operator.

The merge semantics come from Claude Code's documentation, not from code in the tree. Suggested fix: refuse the compile when the user `settings.json` has a `sandbox` block, the same way a non-macOS platform or a malformed value is refused. If you would rather accept the risk, record it as a ceiling in ADR 0191.

https://github.com/AlexisBalayre/pupitre/blob/d53f9f675930a5cc50f12eb035d4cb515875d902/src/core/profile-compiler.service.ts#L1359-L1423

findings.description: The new `allowWrite` entry `join(homedir(), '.pupitre', 'slots')` lets a sandboxed worker's `pup session test` take part in the machine-wide slot protocol. That protocol decides whether a holder is alive with `process.kill(pid, 0)` and treats any error as a dead holder. As I recall it, Claude Code's macOS sandbox profile is deny-default and allows signals only with `(target same-sandbox)`. Each Bash call is its own sandbox instance, and the gate's `pup` process runs unsandboxed. So from inside the sandbox, `kill(pid, 0)` on the gate's pid or another worker's pid returns EPERM. `isAlive` then answers false. `liveHolders` reclaims that live holder's `slot-N.lock`, and `waitingGates` unlinks a waiting gate's `.wait` file. The trigger is a sandboxed worker committing, so its pre-commit hook runs `pup session test`, while a gate holds a slot or waits for one. The worker deletes the gate's slot or wait file and runs its tests beside the gate. That breaks decision 140 (a gate's run has the machine to itself) and gate-before-worker ordering, and the machine is over-subscribed. Nothing reports any of this. Before this change the same call failed to write the slots dir with EPERM, `isUnwritable` matched, and the tests ran slot-less without touching anyone's files. ADR 0191 does not mention the slot handling; its ceiling 3 covers only symlinks planted in the slots dir.

refuted_findings.description: Under `workerSandbox`, the hook walks the path text it receives, but Claude Code's Edit/Write may trim the path before opening it (its `expandPath` calls `path.trim()`). The control-character check is `jq -e '.tool_input.file_path | test("[[:cntrl:]]") | not'`. It refuses tab and newline but lets a trailing U+0020, U+00A0, U+2028/2029 or U+3000 through. Trigger: sandboxed Bash runs `ln -s <main>/.pupitre/project.yml <wt>/src/x.ts` (a compiled hook in the store works as a target too). Then Write is called with file_path `<wt>/src/x.ts ` (trailing space). The hook's walk tests `<wt>/src/x.ts `: `-L` is false, `-e` is false, so it hits `break`. Scope-in `^src/.*$` matches, so the hook exits 0. The tool trims the path to `<wt>/src/x.ts`, follows the link outside the sandbox, and overwrites the main checkout's project.yml (or a hook that runs unsandboxed). This only applies if hooks get the raw `tool_input`, not an already-expanded copy (Claude Code internals, not verifiable statically). The author's own newline fix assumes hooks get the raw input.
refuted_findings.refutation: The finding depends on PreToolUse hooks seeing the raw, untrimmed file_path. Claude Code's Edit and Write backfill the observable input that hooks receive with `expandPath(file_path)`. That is the same trim and normalize the tool applies before opening the file, so the hook walks `<wt>/src/x.ts` and `[ -L ]` blocks it. This rests on knowledge of Claude Code 2.1.x internals; it could not be checked in the tree. The suggested regex would be harmless extra hardening, but it fixes no reachable bug.

process_issues.description: Round 5 budget: conventions, docs, context, simplicity and maintainability were skipped per §4. spec was skipped (no spec source), and workflow-safety was skipped (no workflow change).

Both surviving importants rest on Claude Code and macOS internals (the seatbelt signal rule; how settings arrays merge across sources) that a static CI review cannot probe, so both are capped at medium confidence.
